title: Nasdaq-100 Falls Into Correction as Investors Question AI Spending
excerpt: The tech-heavy index closed 10.4% below its October record in its third correction this year, with chip stocks leading a selloff driven by doubts over AI returns ahead of the midterms.
body:
• The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday at 27,989.82, 10.4% below its October 6 record close of 31,224.47 — a technical correction, and its third drop of at least 10% from a peak this year, according to Dow Jones Market Data via MarketWatch.
  • The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.1% on Monday and the S&P 500 fell 0.5%, while chip stocks led the decline, with Intel down another 8.8%.
  • Strategists say the driver is a repricing of AI returns: investors are questioning whether heavy borrowing for data centres will be paid back adequately.
  • Morgan Stanley says the broader correction that began in June is in its "final innings," with Tuesday's midterm elections a clearing event — a strategist view, not a market outcome.

US technology stocks fell into correction territory on Monday as investors questioned the returns on artificial intelligence spending a day before the midterm elections. The Nasdaq-100 closed at 27,989.82, down 10.4% from its October 6 record-high close of 31,224.47, according to Dow Jones Market Data reported by MarketWatch. A fall of 10% or more from a recent high is the standard definition of a correction. It is the index's third such drop this year.

The day in numbers

The selling was concentrated in technology. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.1% on Monday, leaving it 8.8% below its October 6 peak, while the S&P 500 ended down 0.5%, MarketWatch reported. Most of the S&P 500's 11 sectors were positive on the day, with technology pulling the major indexes lower, according to Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group. Chip stocks bore the brunt: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 3.4%, Micron Technology declined 5.78% and Advanced Micro Devices fell 7.52%, according to market data reported by BigGo Finance. Intel dropped another 8.8% on Monday after a negative reception to its earnings last week, and its stock has fallen 57.4% since a record close of $140.94 on June 22, MarketWatch reported.

"The main root of it is people are questioning some of the assumptions they made about AI."

— Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, to MarketWatch

Why AI spending is the fault line

For much of the past few years, the working assumption was that all money spent on artificial intelligence was well spent, Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, told MarketWatch. The question now, he said, is whether the borrowings behind the data-centre and infrastructure buildout will be paid back adequately. That repricing has been building for weeks: last month the Nasdaq-100 shed more than $2.5 trillion in market value and was on the brink of correction territory as investors grew wary of Big Tech's AI spending while awaiting evidence of stronger returns, Reuters reported. Investors are no longer overlooking free-cash-flow shortfalls, Morgan Stanley's Michael Wilson said, in a market where earnings durability and cash conversion matter more.

The midterm overhang

The November 3 midterm elections are the week's other variable. Morgan Stanley strategists said the broader US market correction that began in June is in its "final innings" and that the elections should help remove a major market overhang, Reuters reported. About 60% of Russell 3000 stocks have already fallen at least 20% since June, Wilson noted, and large-cap stocks have typically gained 15% in the six months following election results, with a Democratic sweep already priced in by investors, according to the bank. The bigger post-vote risks Morgan Stanley named were renewed military escalation with Iran or new tariffs.

What to watch

The Nasdaq-100 is still up 10.9% for the year through Monday, according to FactSet data cited by MarketWatch — a correction inside a rising year, not a bear market. Sosnick cautioned that investors are already fully invested in technology names, leaving less cash to buy dips, and that stocks priced for perfection have to deliver it. The election results, a busy earnings week, and whether chip stocks hold their levels will decide whether this correction is the last stage of the slump, as Morgan Stanley argues, or the start of a deeper repricing of the AI trade.
